opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we spend a lot of time on, because almost every government we talk to is asking that exact question.

I think the honest answer is that for most countries, training a frontier foundation model completely from scratch isn't the best use of their resources. It's enormously expensive. It's not just compute; it's talent, data pipelines, and the ongoing cost of keeping up, because the frontier moves every few months. If you build one model and then stop investing, you're obsolete within a year. So the question isn't really "can we build one?" It's "can we sustain this indefinitely, and is that where our advantage lies?"

What countries actually care about, when you dig in, is sovereignty. They want control over their data. They want the model running on infrastructure they trust, ideally within their borders. They want it to speak their languages well and understand their culture, their legal system, their institutions. And they don't want to depend on a single foreign vendor who could change terms, change the model, or cut them off.

You can get most of that without starting from zero. That's where we see our role. We build strong base models, we're very open about deploying them privately, on-prem, in a country's own data centers or their national cloud, and then we work with them to adapt those models. That means fine-tuning on local language data, building the retrieval systems that connect the model to government and enterprise knowledge, and making sure the security posture meets their requirements. The country owns the deployment and the data, and they get the benefit of a frontier-grade model.

We've also put a lot into multilingual work. A lot of the world has been underserved by models that are essentially English-first, and that's a real equity issue. If your citizens can't use these tools well in their own language, you get left behind economically.

So I'd frame it as a partnership with real sovereignty built in, rather than a binary between "build your own" and "rent from a big American lab." And for the handful of countries that do want deep domestic capability, we're happy to help there too: training local talent, co-developing models, transferring know-how. The goal is for them to come out the other side stronger, not more dependent.

r001.rationale: The response mentions multilingual work and fine-tuning with local language data, but does not describe partnerships with local companies or commitments to sustained investment in countries’ languages.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the question itself has changed a lot over the past couple of years. When we started, the conversation with governments was mostly, "Should we even care about this?" Now it's, "We care, and we need to figure out how to own it." Almost every country we talk to has arrived at the view that AI is going to be critical infrastructure, in the same way that energy or telecom is, and they're uncomfortable with the idea of that infrastructure being entirely controlled by two or three companies headquartered in one place.

So the instinct to build their own model is a very understandable one. The problem is that it's extraordinarily expensive and extraordinarily hard. It's not just capital for compute, although that's a big piece. It's the talent, it's the data pipelines, it's the evaluation infrastructure, it's the years of accumulated know-how about what breaks and why. And the frontier keeps moving. So you can spend a billion dollars and eighteen months and end up with something that's already two generations behind by the time it ships. We've seen that story play out a few times now.

Where I think Cohere fits is that we're trying to offer a middle path. We're not saying "just use our API and trust us." And we're not saying "go build it from scratch and good luck." We're saying, look, we'll bring the frontier model, and critically, you can run it entirely inside your own borders, on your own infrastructure, with your own data, under your own control. The weights sit on your machines. Nothing leaves. And then on top of that, we'll work with you to adapt it, so the model actually speaks your languages well, understands your legal system, your institutions, your context. That's where sovereignty really lives, in my view. It's less about whether you trained the base model yourself and more about whether you control where it runs, what it learns from, and who gets to turn it off.

The other thing I'd say is that being Canadian, and being independent, actually matters here in a way that I didn't fully anticipate early on. When you're talking to a government in Europe or Asia or the Middle East, the fact that we're not a hyperscaler, that we don't have a cloud business we're trying to lock you into, that we're not tied to the strategic interests of any one superpower, that's become a genuine differentiator. Countries want a partner, not a dependency.

So my honest view is that for the vast majority of nations, building a fully homegrown frontier model is probably not the right use of resources. But building the capability around it, the talent, the deployment infrastructure, the domain-specific adaptation, that absolutely is. And that's what we try to enable. We'd rather be the thing that makes a country's AI strategy possible than the thing it's beholden to.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Cohere will work with governments to adapt models for their languages, but does not present partnerships with local companies or describe sustained investment in those countries’ languages.

astra-6.text:
I think countries need to decide which parts of the technology they really need to own and control. Is it the data? The infrastructure? The ability to deploy a model independently and adapt it to their language and their institutions? Those are different requirements from building a foundation model from scratch.

There are good reasons to invest in domestic research and talent. But I don’t think every country needs to reproduce the entire stack to benefit from AI or have sovereignty over how it’s used. You can work with a partner and still have control over where your data lives, who can access it, and how the system operates.

The role I see for Cohere is to help make that possible: bring the underlying models and expertise, then work with local organizations to turn that into useful capabilities. The goal should be to build capacity within the country, so it can deploy and adapt the technology for its own needs. I think that’s a much more productive starting point than treating it as a binary choice between building everything yourself and depending entirely on somebody else.

r001.rationale: The response describes working with local organizations to build local capacity and adapt technology, but does not present Cohere’s partnerships as sustained investment in those countries’ languages within its models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think countries are trying to answer a very reasonable question: how do we benefit from this technology while retaining control over our data and our infrastructure? Building a foundation model from scratch is one way to approach that, but it’s a huge investment, and it’s an ongoing investment. You don’t train a model once and then you’re done.

The role we can play is to give countries another path: partner with us on the underlying technology, but deploy it in an environment they control, with their data staying where they need it to stay. Then work with local companies and developers to adapt it to their languages, their institutions, and their needs.

I think the important distinction is between having sovereignty over how you use AI and having to build every component yourself. You can have meaningful control while partnering. And that lets you put more of your investment into actually making the technology useful for your economy and your public services.

r001.rationale: The response says Cohere would work with local companies and developers to adapt the technology to local languages, but does not present this as a commitment to sustained investment in those countries’ languages within its models.
